clue.text: Maintain United pub from former days

parts.note: U is the usual abbreviation for United in team names
PH, public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub
something from former days is old

explanation.surface: A football supporter keeps up loyalty to a team and a pub from the old days.
explanation.definitionFit: To uphold a decision or tradition is to keep it in force, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Best in series!

parts.note: a ... is a sensational, outstanding thing, and printers also call the exclamation mark that closes the clue a ...

explanation.surface: A critic hails one episode as the highlight of a television run.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings: the episode that is a screamer (a stunner), and the exclamation mark itself, which printers nickname a screamer.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses screamer for anything thrilling or excellent, and printers' jargon for the exclamation mark.

clue.text: Blemish on bit of animation unknown? Hardly

parts.note: a scar is a blemish on the skin
a cel is one transparent sheet painted for a frame of cartoon animation
Y is one of the algebraic unknowns x, y, z

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cartoon frame really has a mark on it, and is told: hardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean only just, or almost not, as in 'could hardly see'.

clue.text: Fool enters motorway heading for furthest mountain region

indicators.note: the fool goes into the motorway letters, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI in crosswords
an ass is a fool

indicators.note: the head, or first letter, of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: A clown drives onto the motorway, bound for the most distant mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: MI stands for the M1, the motorway running north from London.
explanation.definitionFit: A massif is a compact group of mountains forming a distinct block of high ground.

clue.text: Endangered marine feature unregulated first to last

indicators.note: the opening letter is shifted from the front of the word to its end

parts.note: something unregulated is free of controls

explanation.surface: A conservationist warns that a threatened sea habitat is left unregulated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to last' moves the F of FREE to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral reefs are a marine habitat widely described as under threat from warming seas.

clue.text: Unhappy over limits on cruise provider

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the second

parts.note: sour can mean bad-tempered or unhappy

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A passenger is grumpy about the restrictions placed on a holiday cruise.
explanation.definitionFit: A source is where something comes from, so it supplies or provides it.

clue.text: Branch of mathematics laid out in grey tome

indicators.note: letters laid out afresh are arranged in a new order

explanation.surface: A mathematical subject is set out in a dull grey textbook.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometry, the study of shapes and space, is one of the main fields of maths.

clue.text: Disinclined to fight, provided I brought in quiet account

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

indicators.note: the words for provided and I are brought into the middle of the account letters

parts.note: if means provided, as in 'if it rains'

explanation.surface: A peaceable person explains that, provided they speak, it will be a quiet account.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacific in its older sense means peaceable, inclined to make peace rather than war.

clue.text: This is involved in feminine worship

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go in the middle of the abbreviation

parts.note: FEM is the grammatical abbreviation for feminine

indicators.note: involved means twisted or tangled, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that this is part of the worship of the feminine.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetishism is the worship of an object believed to hold magical power, or excessive devotion generally.

clue.text: School has expert around to be source of solution

indicators.note: the school has the expert's letters placed around it
the school has the expert's letters placed around it

parts.note: an ace is an expert
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A school boasts a star teacher who is supposedly the answer to its problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has ... around' puts the expert around the school. 'solution' hides its chemical sense: a liquid with something dissolved in it; Eton is a famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetone is a common solvent, the liquid in which substances are dissolved to make a chemical solution.

clue.text: Initial moves regarding stage performers (name withheld) around end of crusade

parts.note: over can mean about or regarding, as in 'a row over money'

indicators.note: the trimmed performers go around the single letter
N, the abbreviation for name, is removed

parts.note: turns are individual acts in a variety show

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An article about anonymous stage artists touring the scene of a crusade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'name withheld' drops N from TURNS to leave TURS; 'around' puts that around E, the end of 'crusade'. Turns are acts in a British variety show.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtures are opening approaches or proposals made to start a negotiation or relationship.

clue.text: University engaged in class meeting

indicators.note: the university letter is engaged, held, inside the class word

parts.note: a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A university student takes part in a class gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a meeting or assembly held for open discussion.

clue.text: French writer of the French majority? Not quite

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'

indicators.note: the word falls just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: the mass of people is the majority

explanation.surface: A question whether one French author is the favourite of most French readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo.

clue.text: Capable? Sadly ineffective, having dropped last two

indicators.note: sadly signals the letters are in a sorry, jumbled state
the final pair of letters of the word is removed

explanation.surface: A manager wonders if a worker is up to it, finding them sadly useless since losing two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having dropped last two' takes VE from INEFFECTIVE; 'Sadly' scrambles the rest, INEFFECTI.
explanation.definitionFit: Efficient and capable both describe someone who does a job competently.

clue.text: No McMeals dished up at a shared table

indicators.note: food dished up is served out, a hint that these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Diners eating together are told no fast-food meals will be served.
explanation.definitionFit: Commensal comes from Latin for 'at the same table', describing those who eat together.

clue.text: The writer runs railway, welcoming one on board with pleasure

parts.note: the writer of the clue refers to themself as me
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: the railway welcomes, takes in, the letter for one
a passenger on board is inside the vehicle, confirming one piece goes inside another

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A writer boasts of running a railway and gladly welcoming each passenger aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Merrily means cheerfully, gladly, doing something with pleasure.

clue.text: Frenchman is King? Remains in a confused state

parts.note: M is short for monsieur, a Frenchman
HM, His Majesty, refers to a king
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether a Frenchman is king, followed by the remark that things remain in disarray.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishmash is a confused jumble or muddle of things.

clue.text: Military leader with power invested in army of troops

parts.note: CO, commanding officer, is a military leader

indicators.note: power is placed within, as if clothed or vested in, the other word

parts.note: an army of people is a great many
P is the physics abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A commander given power over an army of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A company is a body of soldiers, an army unit of around a hundred troops.

clue.text: One fellow gets embraced by stylish sort

indicators.note: the first pieces are hugged by, placed inside, the stylish word

parts.note: classy means stylish
I is the Roman numeral for one
F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS

explanation.surface: A man finds himself hugged by an elegant type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' looks like a noun, a type of person; here it is the verb, to arrange into groups.
explanation.definitionFit: To classify things is to sort them into categories.

clue.text: Sack secretary that's upset about it as a sort of stimulus

indicators.note: the turned letters go about, around, the word it
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read from the bottom up

parts.note: to sack is to fire
a PA is a personal assistant or secretary

explanation.surface: Firing a secretary who is upset about something serves as a kind of spur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reads the sacking and secretary bottom to top as APERIF, and 'about' wraps that round the clue's 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is a drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Spanish city unhappily regressing — staff about to follow

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: alas is an exclamation of sorrow, said unhappily
to man a post is to staff it
CA, circa, means about

explanation.surface: A Spanish city is sadly slipping back, with staff set to follow shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: Salamanca is a university city in western Spain.

clue.text: Content of journal is somewhat flexible

indicators.note: the contents of the phrase are what lies inside it

explanation.surface: A reader finds what a magazine prints is fairly adaptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Lissom means supple and lithe, bending easily.

clue.text: Note from the past? Just about

parts.note: early can describe something from an earlier time, as in early music

explanation.surface: Someone recognises a note from long ago, more or less.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly and just about both mean almost.

clue.text: Change what anthem and theorem have in common

parts.words: what anthem and theorem have in common
parts.note: both words close on the same two letters, E then M, which is the shared feature named

explanation.surface: A puzzle asks how to amend the feature a song and a proof share.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words finish with EM, so what they share is an 'EM end'.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct or alter it.

clue.text: In Germany, it is German to refrain

parts.note: D is the international vehicle code for Germany, so German
in German, 'it is' is 'es ist'

explanation.surface: A traveller notes that in Germany abstaining is the German way.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to stop or hold back from doing something.

clue.text: Microphone capturing American singing?

indicators.note: one piece captures, encloses, the other

parts.note: mic is short for microphone
US means American, as in US troops

explanation.surface: A microphone records an American, perhaps a singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing is one example of music, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Casket regularly lost mass

indicators.note: letters at regular intervals, every third, are lost from the word

explanation.surface: A casket keeps losing its weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly lost' removes the third and sixth letters, S and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A cake can be a compact block of something, as in a cake of soap or of mud.

clue.text: A crime's involving brazen behaviour from these killers

indicators.note: the word for crimes involves, takes inside, the cheek

parts.note: crime's read as crime is, or as the plural of sin, gives SINS
sass is cheeky, brazen talk

explanation.surface: An offence marked by cheek comes from these murderers.
explanation.definitionFit: Assassins are killers, especially of prominent people.

clue.text: Swimming aid: no risk losing one at sea (Spanish article)

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled
a letter is lost from the phrase

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
el is Spanish for 'the'

explanation.surface: A swimmer reassures that a flotation device carries no risk at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing one' takes I from NO RISK; 'at sea' scrambles NORSK.
explanation.definitionFit: A snorkel is a breathing tube used by swimmers face-down in the water.

clue.text: Theatrical area enshrining most of old silly things

indicators.note: to enshrine is to hold within, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: the flies are the space above a theatre stage where scenery hangs

indicators.note: the last letter is dropped, leaving most of the word

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: An old theatre area is said to hold daft relics.
explanation.walkthrough: The flies are the space above a stage. Follies were also lavish theatrical revues, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Follies are foolish acts or ideas, silly things done.
